concepts.definition: An agreed meaning for a measure, including population, grain, numerator, denominator, time, exclusions and owner.
concepts.example: Unit defect rate 1/20=5% differs from inspections-with-defect 1/2=50%.

concepts.definition: The relationships showing how a result depends on upstream data and transformations.
concepts.example: A displayed 5% depends on acceptedA/C quantities, aggregation and a stated cut-off.

concepts.definition: Elapsed time from a specified request point to a usable result.
concepts.example: 30 seconds waiting+5 executing+10 presenting=45 seconds experienced.

concepts.definition: Uneven work distribution in which a few tasks take much longer than the others.
concepts.example: One hot-key partition processes 90 rows while three others process 3, 3, 4.

concepts.definition: Stored query output that can be reused instead of recomputing the query.
concepts.example: A repeated query may return quickly from cached results without a new execution profile.

concepts.definition: Completed work per unit of time under a stated workload and measurement window.
concepts.example: 12 queries per minute says something different from one query taking 5 seconds.

concepts.definition: A comparison that holds relevant conditions stable while changing a stated hypothesis and measuring agreed outcomes.
concepts.example: Compare one capacity setting with fixed query, data, cache policy and 12-user workload.

concepts.definition: The slower end of the request-latency distribution, beyond the typical or median experience.
concepts.example: A median 5 s can coexist with 10% of requests exceeding 60 s.

concepts.definition: A condition applied to aggregated groups, rather than to each input row.

concepts.example: No. Check the agreed request count and strict timing predicate directly, preserving failures and missing measurements.

beats.title: 5% and 50% can both be correct
beats.outcome: Name the numerator and denominator before comparing reports.
beats.explanation: A has 12 inspected units and 1 defective; C has 8 and 0. The unit defect rate is 5%, while half the inspections found any defect. A [[dbxfe-m05-metric-concept|metric contract]] names which question the report answers. A fast dashboard titled “quality 50%” is still ambiguous. Resolve meaning before tuning the query that calculates it.

samajh.text: Ek question hai kitne units defective nikle; doosra hai kitni inspections mein koi defect mila. Same records se dono numbers aa sakte hain. Denominator badla toh question badal gaya. Sirf “quality” label se reader ko guess karna padega; naam mein quantity clear rakho.
samajh.mapping: The counted unit determines the meaning of the rate.
samajh.boundary: Neither metric is universally preferable; the decision and contract choose it.

handbook.markdown:
Write the metric as a sentence before SQL: accepted defective units divided by accepted inspected units, grouped by plant and business day, with an explicit correction and exclusion policy. Name the owner who approves changes. For a zero denominator, our example returns undefined rather than 0%, because no inspected population establishes a rate.

The same source supports another metric: inspections with at least one defect divided by inspections. A contributes one positive inspection and C one negative, so the result is 50%. That measure may answer a useful operational question, but it is not interchangeable with the 5% unit rate. A dashboard should label both clearly if both are shown.

Also record the time basis: event time, ingestion cut-off and business-day zone can differ. Is historical reporting restated after corrections or shown as known at the meeting? Either can be coherent if labeled and owned. Product semantic-layer tools can help reuse a definition, but they cannot negotiate this business agreement. Reconcile representative rows before treating visual agreement as correctness.

beats.recap: A number has meaning only with its population and denominator.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: The dashboard is the last mile
beats.outcome: Trace a visible metric back to accepted records and its freshness.
beats.explanation: A dashboard presents the result; it does not establish the result’s trustworthiness. Follow [[dbxfe-m05-serving-concept|data lineage]] backward from 5% to totals 1/20, to accepted A and C, and to retained evidence. Show freshness and exclusions beside the number. A query can run today over a previous snapshot, so execution time alone is not a data freshness label.

handbook.markdown:
Pick one displayed figure and explain every dependency needed to reproduce it. The accepted population determines which inspections count. The metric logic determines the numerator and denominator. The serving query applies the requested filters. The dashboard formats the result and should make its time/coverage limits visible.

The diagram uses three names from reliable data foundations. Inspection B is a conflicting record held out of the accepted state, with its reason, until it is resolved; replay re-runs the retained deliveries to rebuild that state; and `stale_previous` is the publication status that keeps the previous report on show, labelled, while new evidence blocks its replacement.

For Cinderline, a 5% display can be correct for the last verified 1/20 snapshot while a later correction remains unresolved. Label it previous or stale according to the publication policy; do not relabel the latest successful query execution as the latest accepted source state. This matters when people act at shift change.

Databricks SQL supplies analytical interfaces and execution resources. Reusable metric definitions can reduce copy-paste drift, but a central definition still needs an owner, representative tests and an explicit change process. Lineage helps locate dependencies; it does not prove the source is complete or the business rule is right. In a review, ask the analyst to trace one number to rows and state which excluded inputs or unresolved issues are not represented. That demonstration is more informative than a screenshot alone.

beats.recap: Trace the KPI to rows and show the data cut-off, not only query time.
beats.changeNote: 1.1.0: handbook now introduces Inspection B, replay and the stale_previous status before the diagram relies on them, and writes the snapshot ratio as 1/20; the evidence node names B as the conflicting inspection. The explanation and check are unchanged; earlier answers and notes are retained and a completed beat is marked revised.

beats.title: The same 45 seconds can mean different work
beats.outcome: Decompose end-to-end delay before choosing a remedy.
beats.explanation: Separate waiting, execution and presentation. RunA spends 30 seconds queued, 5 executing and 10 transferring/rendering; runC spends 0, 35 and 10. Both feel like 45 seconds, but the dominant delay differs. Define [[dbxfe-m05-latency-concept|latency]] at the user boundary, then inspect the stage that explains the difference before proposing more capacity or a query rewrite.

samajh.text: Clinic mein aaj 45 minute lage: 30 minute line mein, 5 minute doctor ke saath, 10 minute dawai ke counter par. Kal bhi 45 minute lage, par line zero thi aur doctor ke saath 35 minute. Dono din “slow” lage, lekin ilaaj alag hai: ek din extra counter chahiye tha, doosre din consultation hi lambi thi. Query ka bhi waise hi breakdown karo: queue, execution aur result render ko alag alag dekho, phir remedy chuno.
samajh.mapping: The line is queueing, the consultation is execution, and the medicine counter is result transfer and rendering.
samajh.boundary: A query profile measures only its own scope; the clinic clock includes travel that a profile never sees.

handbook.markdown:
Define measurement start and end before comparing runs. A user may include dashboard loading, waiting for compute, query planning/execution, result transfer and browser rendering. A query profile has its own scope. Neither is wrong, but subtracting differently scoped durations can produce an invented bottleneck.

Our ledger holds execution and presentation constant for A versusB, isolating a queue difference. That suggests investigating peak concurrency, workload arrival and capacity. B versusC instead changes execution while queue and presentation remain equal; inspect the changed join and its rows/operators. Neither table proves the ultimate root cause without run evidence.

Record query text, input snapshot, warehouse type/configuration, user population, cache conditions and failures. Compare representative cases rather than one lucky run. A remedy that makes execution faster may have little effect when most user time is waiting or rendering. Conversely, reducing queues will not repair a multiplying join. The next beat looks inside execution while preserving the end-to-end view.

**Startup and queueing are waiting, not work.** If the warehouse was stopped, the first morning request pays a compute startup delay before any planning begins; if twelve refreshes arrive together, later ones wait in a queue for a slot. Both appear inside the user’s 45 seconds and neither appears in the execution operators. Record whether the warehouse was already running, how many queries were queued at arrival, and how long each waited; a quiet-hour test with a warm warehouse cannot reproduce the 08:00 experience. The remedy for startup (keep it warm, or schedule the first refresh) differs from the remedy for a queue (capacity, scheduling or fewer redundant refreshes), and both differ from a query rewrite.

beats.recap: Equal total latency can hide different bottlenecks; compare its components.
beats.changeNote: 1.1.0: handbook deepened (“Startup and queueing are waiting, not work”); optional Samajh analogy added. The explanation, visual and check are unchanged; earlier answers and notes are retained and a completed beat is marked revised.

beats.title: Inspect rows, imbalance and spilled work
beats.outcome: Connect profile evidence to a bounded query hypothesis.
beats.explanation: Execution evidence can reveal a multiplying join, [[dbxfe-m05-execution-concept|skew]], or spill from execution memory to disk. These are different mechanisms. A hot key can leave one task working while others finish; a large intermediate relation can consume memory even when the final result is tiny. Inspect rows and task distributions before treating a larger resource as the explanation.

handbook.markdown:
Start with correctness: compare input and output row counts around joins. An unexpectedly large relation may reflect the many-to-many behavior taught in transformations. Next inspect whether work is balanced. If one partition or task receives much more data, adding parallel resources may leave much of that capacity idle while the hot task dominates.

Spill occurs when execution work moves from memory to disk. It can accompany joins, sorts and aggregations. Connect spill metrics to the relevant operator and data volume before deciding between reducing work, changing distribution or testing capacity. A tiny final result can hide a large intermediate relation.

The visual numbers are synthetic and do not prescribe a tuning threshold. A real profile needs permissions and actual run context. Operator labels from a video about another Spark execution engine illustrate concepts; they do not establish Databricks Photon implementation or benchmark claims. The remedy should be a falsifiable hypothesis: for example, correcting the join grain should reduce intermediate rows while preserving independently expected totals. Measure the result rather than accepting an operator-name explanation.

**Pruning and shuffle are two different questions about the same plan.** Pruning asks how much data the scan could skip: a predicate on the plant or date can let the engine avoid files or partitions it does not need, so compare bytes and files scanned with the population the filter actually names. A shuffle asks how much data had to move: a join or aggregation on a key redistributes rows so matching keys meet, and the exchange volume tells you the size of the relation being moved. A scan that reads everything for a one-plant answer suggests a missed pruning opportunity; a large exchange feeding a tiny result suggests a multiplied or skewed intermediate relation. Diagnose each with rows in and out, then form one falsifiable hypothesis per observation.

beats.recap: Explain the intermediate work; final result size is only one observation.
beats.changeNote: 1.1.0: handbook deepened (“Pruning and shuffle are two different questions about the same plan”). The explanation, visual and check are unchanged; earlier answers and notes are retained and a completed beat is marked revised.

beats.title: A cached answer is a different experiment
beats.outcome: Identify cache conditions that confound performance comparisons.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-m05-cache-concept|result cache]] can avoid work altogether. Comparing a cold execution with a cached answer does not isolate the effect of a SQL rewrite. Record cache conditions deliberately; a missing profile may be consistent with cached results. Restarting a warehouse alone is not a universal cold-cache guarantee because cache layers and lifecycles differ.

handbook.markdown:
Choose what you want to measure: uncached execution efficiency, repeated-query user experience, or the realistic mix of both. Then hold or document the cache policy accordingly. A valid workload test can include warm caches, but the comparison must use a comparable basis and disclose it.

Databricks documents separate UI, result and disk cache behavior, with different lifecycle details. In particular serverless remote result caching can survive a warehouse restart. Therefore “we restarted” is not enough evidence that every cache was cold. AI/BI dashboards also have their own behavior; a SQL editor observation is not automatically a dashboard observation.

A profile may be unavailable for a cached query, while access permissions can also govern what the user sees. Record the exact observation rather than concluding that the engine performed zero work or that monitoring is broken. In the synthetic A/B/C experiment, cache conditions are held fixed by assumption. In a real test they must be verified and recorded alongside query, data, configuration and concurrency. Do not disable useful caching in production merely to imitate a benchmark.

beats.recap: State the cache policy; a faster reuse path does not prove a faster execution plan.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Faster one query and serving many are different goals
beats.outcome: Distinguish latency, throughput and concurrency in a capacity decision.
beats.explanation: Concurrency is simultaneous work; latency is time to a result; [[dbxfe-m05-capacity-concept|throughput]] is completed work over time. Warehouse size and cluster count address different capacity dimensions, and serverless behavior differs from classic/pro. Test the morning population and a quiet period. Extra capacity can reduce a queue without fixing a bad join, or add idle cost without meeting the tail-latency target.

handbook.markdown:
A system can be fast for one query and still queue under simultaneous demand. It can also complete many small queries while one important long query misses its deadline. Specify the workload population and distribution instead of relying only on averages.

Current warehouse documentation distinguishes resources per cluster from scaling multiple clusters and describes different management for serverless versus classic/pro. The lesson does not turn those differences into a universal sizing rule or guarantee of proportional speedup. Inspect queue and spill evidence in the actual target environment, then test one justified change.

For Cinderline, include the twelve-user morning refresh pattern and a two-user quiet check. Measure allowed workload completed, latency distribution, failures and the full agreed cost basis. A candidate that improves the median but leaves a critical tail unresolved may not meet the objective. A quiet-period test detects idle consumption that a short peak test would miss. Synthetic cost units in the next beat are comparison arithmetic only, not rates, quotations or an instruction to provision paid resources.

beats.recap: Capacity must serve the workload distribution, not only a single fast query.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: Change one hypothesis and keep the denominator
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-m05-experiment-concept|controlled experiment]] needs a fixed workload and an agreed success criterion. Hold query, input snapshot, cache policy and concurrency comparable; change one capacity or query hypothesis. Record failures and excluded work. A faster run that quietly drops hard queries changes the denominator of success, just as dropping inspections can distort a quality metric.

handbook.markdown:
Write the hypothesis in a form that could be wrong. “Peak queueing is the main delay; changing this capacity setting should reduce queue time without changing query results” is testable. “Make it faster” is not specific enough to select evidence. Preserve input and expected output so performance work cannot silently change correctness.

For each run record workload size, completion/failure counts, latency distribution, queue/execution breakdown and the agreed usage/cost basis. Include test duration and idle/start behavior where relevant. If data movement or another charge is excluded, say so. Do not present a synthetic unit or list price as a customer’s total cost.

Multiple simultaneous changes can still be useful exploratory work, but label the conclusion accordingly. A follow-up can isolate the most plausible factor. A real experiment also needs an authorized budget/stop condition and an owner; none is executed here. The applied result next deliberately improves one statistic while failing the actual objective, so the learner must report both rather than choosing whichever number looks favorable.

beats.recap: Fix the workload and success rule before changing a performance hypothesis.
beats.changeNote: New teacher-first explanation and worked visual; earlier lesson completion does not complete this beat.

beats.title: A better median can still fail the goal
beats.outcome: Read a performance result against its original acceptance criterion.
beats.explanation: The candidate lowers median latency from 8 seconds to 5, but 10% of requests still exceed 60 seconds. The goal was 95% under 15 seconds. That goal is not met: at most 90% can be under 15. Report the median improvement, unresolved [[dbxfe-m05-transfer-concept|tail latency]] and higher test cost together, then choose evidence for the slow subgroup.

handbook.markdown:
Evaluate the agreed criterion directly. Out of 100 hypothetical requests, at least 10 are slower than 60 seconds and therefore slower than 15 seconds. The goal allows no more than 5 requests outside 15 seconds. Even without knowing the other 90 exact timings, the candidate cannot meet the stated target.

Report three findings: the typical experience improved, the slow subgroup remains unacceptable, and test cost increased by 30 arbitrary units under the same stated basis. Do not hide any of them behind a single “faster” label. The next investigation should identify which queries/users or operators form the tail and compare queue, skew, spill, data volume and cache evidence.

A customer recommendation might be a targeted follow-up, not automatic rejection of every change or blanket approval of more capacity. Retain the population and failure counts so the next result is comparable. This is a synthetic interpretation exercise, not a vendor benchmark. Review canonical cards on metric meaning, query evidence and capacity, then choose source-backed extensions about profile access and cache/time scope deliberately.

beats.recap: Report against the original threshold; the median cannot certify the tail.
beats.changeNote: 1.1.0: the result table's baseline tail cell, previously "Unresolved", now says the slowest 10% were already above 60 s and the candidate leaves them there. The explanation, handbook and check are unchanged; earlier answers and notes are retained and a completed beat is marked revised.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can aggregate task time exceed wall-clock query duration?
extensionCards.answer: Tasks can run concurrently, and aggregate task time sums their durations.
extensionCards.explanation: Four tasks running for 5 seconds in parallel contribute about 20 task-seconds while that concurrent phase lasts about 5 wall-clock seconds. Scheduling and other overhead add context; do not equate the sums.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Prevents a misleading bottleneck or savings calculation when summed parallel task time is mistaken for elapsed time.

extensionCards.prompt: What access is needed to view a query profile?
extensionCards.answer: Query ownership or at least the documented warehouse monitoring permission.
extensionCards.explanation: The current source specifies ownership or CAN MONITOR on the executing SQL warehouse. A missing view may reflect access or cached execution, so inspect the specific case rather than assuming monitoring failure.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Diagnostic plans need the right observer identity, or a missing profile looks like a missing problem.

extensionCards.prompt: May an approximate percentile alone certify an exact requirement that at least 95% of requests finish strictly under 15 seconds?
extensionCards.answer: No. Check the agreed request count and strict timing predicate directly, preserving failures and missing measurements.
extensionCards.explanation: An [[dbxfe-m05-extension-approximate-percentile-concept|approximate percentile]] is useful for exploring a large timing distribution, but a release condition may require exact counting. The documented function exposes an accuracy setting that changes memory and approximation accuracy. In an original 100-request example, 94 finish below 15 seconds and 6 finish exactly at 15. The strict-under condition has 94 successes, so a 95% target fails even though rounding the times can make the boundary look harmless. Compute the agreed Boolean predicate over the agreed denominator, and state how failures and missing measurements are handled. Use percentile summaries alongside that result rather than silently replacing the contract. This is arithmetic and measurement guidance, not an executed benchmark or a claim about a particular approximation error.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Approximation and threshold-boundary choices must not silently redefine a pass.

extensionCards.prompt: North has inspection quantities 12 and 8. To retain plants totaling at least 20, should WHERE inspected>=20 replace HAVING SUM(inspected)>=20?
extensionCards.answer: No. The row filter drops both North rows; the group filter keeps North's total 20.
extensionCards.explanation: Filter placement changes meaning. Our synthetic input has North inspections 12 and 8, plus South 15. Grouping first produces North 20 and South 15; HAVING SUM(inspected)>=20 keeps North. A WHERE inspected>=20 condition instead removes every input row, because none individually reaches 20. The faster empty result would answer the wrong question. Before moving a condition earlier to reduce work, establish whether it concerns input records or their aggregate. The documented HAVING clause operates on grouped results; its expressions use grouping terms, aggregates or constants. Inspect keys and totals after a rewrite, then measure performance. These expected results are hand-worked, not a claim that either query was run.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A plausible optimization can change the business population instead of merely reducing work.

recap.title: Meaning first, evidence second, one test next
recap.markdown:
**Metric contract → traced rows/freshness → queue/execution/presentation → operator evidence → controlled test → threshold and cost decision.** Review linked core cards before adding extensions. All benchmark-like numbers here are synthetic.

**Next learning action:** continue with C4 Business intelligence and semantic delivery (`#/module/dbxfe-bi`), where the metric contract and freshness cut-off you traced here reach the dashboard reader.

appliedTask.title: Recommend the next experiment
appliedTask.prompt: A peak dashboard waits 30 s, executes 5 s and renders 10 s. A candidate lowers median latency to 5 s but leaves 10% of requests above 60 s and increases cost. The goal is 95% under 15 s. What should the customer hear and what evidence comes next?
appliedTask.modelAnswer: The candidate improves the median but fails the agreed tail criterion and costs more. Inspect the slow subgroup’s queue/execution breakdown and representative profiles, preserving query/data/cache/concurrency conditions; test a targeted hypothesis and measure the same threshold, failures and total cost basis.
appliedTask.reasoning: The recommendation reports all material evidence and directs the next test toward the unresolved delay rather than declaring success from a favorable summary.
